GDC-RR-3913ef0116.title: A pre-post single-arm pilot trial of a digital multicomponent intervention for self-efficacy enhancement among online support groups of primary caregivers of children with neuro-muscular disorders: SEE-NMD protocol.
GDC-RR-3913ef0116.authors: Aziz NI, Khalid W, Khan S.
GDC-RR-3913ef0116.abstract:
Introduction

Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) and Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) are progressive genetic neuromuscular disorders that impose substantial caregiving demands on families. In Pakistan, where disease-modifying therapies remain largely inaccessible, care is predominantly supportive, frequently resulting in psychological distress and diminished caregiver confidence. An individual's belief in their capacity to execute required behaviours, self-efficacy, is a recognised determinant of caregiving quality, yet evidence on caregiver self-efficacy in SMA and DMD within low-resource settings remains sparse. This protocol describes the methods for an exploratory, single-arm, pre-post trial. The trial aims to generate preliminary evidence on changes in self-efficacy following a multicomponent, digitally delivered intervention and its implementation feasibility among primary caregivers of children with SMA and DMD in Pakistan.

Methods and analysis

A single-arm, pre-post study design will recruit primary caregivers of children with SMA and DMD enrolled in the Treat-NMD Registry of Pakistan, with 40 caregivers per condition (80 total) analyzed as separate disease-specific cohorts. An eight-week intervention will be delivered via online support groups, comprising educational video clips, expert-led live sessions, pictorial guides, and progressively tapering audio reminders. The primary outcome, self-efficacy, will be measured using a culturally adapted, content-validated Urdu version of the DMD Caregiver Self-Efficacy Scale (DMD-CSES), assessed at baseline (T0) and eight weeks post-intervention (T1). Pre- and post-intervention scores will be compared using a paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, depending on the data distribution, with analyses conducted in STATA Version 17.

Ethics and dissemination

Ethical approval has been granted by the Ethics Review Committee of Aga Khan University (2025-11875-37040). Verbal informed consent will be obtained from all participants, and confidentiality will be maintained throughout the trial. The findings will be disseminated via peer-reviewed publications, conference presentations, and shared with the Treat-NMD registry network.

Trial registration name and number

NCT07356063, Date of registration: 11/January/2026.

GDC-RR-0754a1641c.title: Mental Health Effects of Social Media Use Among Adolescents Across Educational Stages: A Meta-Analysis.
GDC-RR-0754a1641c.authors: Han C, Meng Y, Yang L.
GDC-RR-0754a1641c.abstract: BackgroundThe link between social media use and adolescent mental health is widely studied, but its variation across developmental stages remains insufficiently clarified. This meta-analysis aimed to compare the differential associations among primary, middle, and high school students.MethodsWe systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Embase, and CNKI up to 1 February 2026. Eligible studies reported correlation coefficients between social media use and mental health in school-aged youth. Analyses were performed using Stata 17.0 with random-effects model, subgroup stratification, heterogeneity testing, publication bias assessment, and leave-one-out sensitivity analysis.ResultsTwelve studies with 15 effect sizes were included. Social media use was significantly associated with worse mental health (r = 0.308, 95%CI: 0.239-0.374, p < 0.001) with high heterogeneity (I<sup>2</sup> = 93.85%). The association differed significantly by stage (Q = 9.72, p = 0.008): strongest in primary school students (r = 0.367), followed by high schoolers (r = 0.334), and weakest in middle schoolers (r = 0.201). No significant publication bias was detected; results were stable.ConclusionsThe association between social media use and mental health varies significantly across educational stages, with primary school students being the most vulnerable. Developmentally tailored prevention and intervention strategies are needed for school-aged youth.

claudeReview.reviewBasis: The abstract as published by Europe PMC on 9 November 2026, plus the Crossref record for DOI 10.1177/13591045261487468. The full text was NOT read: the journal page was not fetched. Every verdict below is therefore about what the abstract states and about the design it describes, not about the paper's internal detail.
claudeReview.proposedTitle: A new meta-analysis says the effect is much bigger. Here is how I decided not to use it.
claudeReview.proposedAngle: A paper landed this week that would help the argument I make for a living, and I am not going to use it. Walking a parent through why is more useful than the number itself, because it is the same test they can apply to the next frightening headline.
claudeReview.oneStory: A meta-analysis published on 6 November reports a correlation between social media use and worse mental health that is far larger than the best powered studies have found, and it would be very convenient for anybody selling a solution.
claudeReview.oneTension: The number is real and peer reviewed, and it still should not change what you believe, because twelve studies pooled with ninety four percent heterogeneity is not stronger evidence than a representative cohort of twenty five thousand.
claudeReview.oneBelief: We judge a finding by its design and its spread, not by whether it points the way we already lean. We publish the ones that are awkward for us, which means we also have to decline the ones that flatter us.
claudeReview.oneTakeaway: When a study says the effect is bigger than you were told, look for two things before you believe it: how many studies went in, and whether they agreed with each other.

claims.claim: The pooled correlation between social media use and worse adolescent mental health was r = 0.308, 95% CI 0.239 to 0.374, p < 0.001.
claims.basis: Stated verbatim in the published abstract. The DOI resolves through Crossref and the online publication date, 6 November 2026, agrees with the index. This verifies what the paper reports, not that the figure is a good estimate of the real world association.

claims.claim: The association varies by educational stage, and primary school students are the most vulnerable group.
claims.basis: The subgroup test is Q = 9.72, p = 0.008, but it is splitting twelve studies and fifteen effect sizes across three school stages. A subgroup analysis on that few studies is badly underpowered and highly sensitive to which study sits in which bin. 'Most vulnerable' is also a clinical claim about children, and the underlying studies are correlational, so the design cannot carry it.

claims.claim: r = 0.308 is a reasonable estimate of the association between adolescent social media use and mental health.
claims.basis: Two reasons for caution, both from the abstract itself. The heterogeneity is I squared = 93.85 percent, which means the twelve studies disagree with each other enormously and a single pooled number describes none of them well. And the search included CNKI alongside the English language databases, so the sample is likely weighted towards Chinese cohorts, which the abstract does not break down. The funder is the National Social Science Foundation of China. None of that makes the figure wrong, and all of it has to be said before it is repeated.

claims.claim: This finding is larger than the association reported by the best powered work in this field.
claims.basis: It is substantially larger than the pooled estimates we have already verified, which sit near beta = 0.061 across 46 studies and 79 effect sizes. But r and a standardised beta are not the same quantity, so the comparison is directional rather than a clean ratio. Do NOT write that it is five or six times bigger. Write that it is much larger and that the metrics differ.

claims.claim: Social media use has mental health effects on adolescents.
claims.basis: The paper's own title says 'Effects' while its methods pool correlation coefficients. The abstract body correctly says 'associated with' throughout. The title overclaims relative to the design, which is worth noting precisely because the title is what gets quoted.

GDC-RR-04ce5786d0.title: Risks and Opportunities in Digital Media Interventions for Youth: A Scientometric Review
GDC-RR-04ce5786d0.authors: Andrews O, Brons ME, Chaplinska I, Nikken P, Ina HK, Mary S, Schuengel C.
GDC-RR-04ce5786d0.abstract: Youth must navigate both the opportunities and risks associated with digital media. Thisscientometric review examined 120 empirical studies on digital media interventions for youthand used the 4C framework (content, contact, conduct, and contract) to map their thematic focus.Scientometric mapping techniques were applied to explore keyword co-occurrence patterns andcollaboration networks. Most interventions addressed either risks or opportunities separately(58.3%), whereas 39.2% combined risks and opportunities within the same 4C dimension. Only2.5% integrated multiple 4C dimensions. Interventions predominantly focused on content andconduct, with limited attention to contact and contract, including topics like social interactions,privacy, digital rights, and commercialization. Collaboration patterns were fragmented, withresearchers working within thematic clusters rather than across them, despite drawing on ashared conceptual foundation. These findings suggest that current interventions cover only partof the 4C framework. Future research should encourage more integrated, cross-dimensionalinterventions and stronger collaboration among researchers.

GDC-RR-d49a029e70.title: Evaluating Human-Robot Interaction With a Socially Assistive Robot in Pediatric Health Care: Mixed Methods Pilot Study.
GDC-RR-d49a029e70.authors: Leoste J, Rakić S, Marmor K, Krinal K, Soostar LH, Vink KM, Käver A, Aasma K, Beatty K, Leoste LB.
GDC-RR-d49a029e70.abstract:
Background

Socially assistive robots are increasingly explored in health care, but evidence from routine pediatric outpatient settings remains limited.

Objective

This study examined how contextual support and human facilitation shaped visitor interaction with the Temi V3 robot and which sociotechnical conditions were associated with practical acceptance according to staff.

Methods

A mixed methods pilot combined structured behavioral observation across baseline, poster support, and staff facilitation conditions with 4 staff focus group interviews. The observation unit was a visitor passage through the lobby zone; the qualitative sample comprised 12 staff members with direct exposure to the robot. Quantitative indicators were analyzed descriptively, and staff interviews underwent deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis.

Results

In total, 675 visitor passages (children: n=398, 59% and adults: n=277, 41%) were recorded (baseline: n=257; poster support: n=160; and staff facilitation: n=258). Looking at the robot increased from 8 (3.1%) passages at baseline to 30 (18.8%) with poster support and 80 (31%) with staff facilitation. Screen or app use increased from 2 (0.8%) passages at baseline to 4 (2.5%) with poster support and 14 (5.4%) with staff facilitation. Observer notes indicated stronger visible responsiveness among children, although age category was not linked to individual behavior codes. Staff emphasized role clarity, child and family value, human mediation, functional reliability, multilingual content, and organizational ownership.

Conclusions

Observed visitor interaction was higher with poster support and staff facilitation than at baseline. These descriptive findings and staff perceptions informed a provisional 4-domain framework comprising role clarity, interaction affordance, social mediation, and organizational embedding. The framework identifies potential implementation priorities; visitors' own experiences and acceptance require direct assessment.

GDC-RR-4cdb28660e.title: Neonatal malaria management: a global survey of current practice.
GDC-RR-4cdb28660e.authors: Sultanli A, Remppis J, Honkpehedji YJ, Reif C, Esen M, Adegnika AA, Bélard S.
GDC-RR-4cdb28660e.abstract:
Background

Neonatal malaria remains underrecognised despite persistent high neonatal mortality in endemic regions. Evidence to guide diagnosis, classification, and treatment during the first 28 days of life is scarce, and neonatal-specific recommendations are largely absent. We conducted an international survey to describe current practices in neonatal malaria management and identify gaps in care.

Methods

We performed an anonymous online survey of healthcare professionals involved in neonatal malaria care between April 2024 and July 2025. The questionnaire, available in English, French, Portuguese, and Spanish, was distributed through professional networks and targeted invitations, assessing screening practices, diagnostic approaches, disease definitions, treatment strategies, dosing approaches, and perceived challenges. Data were analysed descriptively.

Results

A total of 173 respondents from malaria-endemic and non-endemic settings were included; most (91%) were based in sub-Saharan Africa. Most (61%) reported diagnosing neonatal malaria at least once yearly and 39% at least once a month. Most respondents (72%) did not distinguish between asymptomatic and symptomatic neonatal parasitaemia, and half (49%) did not differentiate between uncomplicated or severe malaria in neonates. The most used drugs were intravenous artesunate and artemether-lumefantrine for oral treatment. Among those using oral therapy, 71% reported using paediatric formulations, while 38% crushed tablets prior to administration. Crushed tablets were mostly mixed with water (90%), followed by expressed breast milk (23%) and infant formula (20%). In a case vignette of neonatal malaria, 87% of respondents recommended inpatient management with initial intravenous artesunate (92%) followed by oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (66%) with treatment duration ranging from 1 to 10 days and follow-up within 28 days (33%).

Conclusions

This survey demonstrates consensus in antimalarial drug selection alongside significant practice variation in disease classification and dosing, highlighting the need for evidence-based guidelines and improved access to age-appropriate formulations for neonatal malaria management.

GDC-RR-26d109b285.title: Sensory Literacies in Early Childhood Education: A Multimodal Interaction Analysis of Olfaction‐Enhanced Shared Reading
GDC-RR-26d109b285.authors: Radel James Gacumo, Ingrid Midteide Løkken, Natalia Ingebretsen Kucirkova
GDC-RR-26d109b285.abstract: ABSTRACT Reading in early childhood involves the coordination of multiple senses and modes of meaning‐making. While multimodal literacy research has examined visual, verbal and gestural interaction, the role of the sense of smell in shared reading remains largely unexplored. This study explores how young children engage bodily and emotionally during shared reading of olfaction‐enhanced digital books in early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings. Drawing on video observations of five Norwegian children aged 4–5, the analysis employs multimodal interaction analysis to examine how gesture, gaze, talk and smell intersect during literacy participation. The findings show how olfactory cues became integrated into embodied and collaborative forms of engagement. Children's interactions included moments of curiosity, affective synchrony and sustained attention around olfactory encounters, with smell emerging in some interactions as a semiotic pivot around which sensory perception, affect and interpretation became interconnected. The study suggests that attending to olfactory modes can extend understandings of multimodal literacy by making visible the intersections between digital reading and embodied sensory participation. These insights contribute to discussions of inclusive and holistic approaches to early literacy in ECEC.

GDC-RR-159233af83.title: Implementation of canva-based learning media to develop object-classification skills in children aged 5–6 years
GDC-RR-159233af83.authors: Meiman Sartika Zega, Khairatun Nisa, Novi Cynthia Yusnita
GDC-RR-159233af83.abstract: This study described the implementation of Canva-based learning media to develop object-classification skills among children aged 5–6 years at TK Elpatisia Medan. It used a descriptive qualitative approach involving the principal, the Group B teacher, and 15 children. Data were collected through observation, interviews, and documentation. Data credibility was supported by source and technique triangulation and member checking, while analysis involved data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings indicated that Canva media was implemented through planning, classroom implementation, and evaluation. Visual presentations containing colors, shapes, sizes, and object categories helped make learning more engaging and supported children in comparing and grouping objects. The observations described children as generally able to classify objects by color and type, while classification by shape and size was generally at the level of developing as expected; some children still needed prompts and teacher assistance. Supporting factors included school leadership support, teacher capability, children’s interest in visual materials, and the availability of laptops and a projector. Challenges included unstable internet access, limited devices, distractions, differences in children’s learning pace, and preparation time. The study concludes that Canva can serve as a useful visual learning medium when accompanied by teacher guidance and adequate preparation.

GDC-RR-d1f9996f06.title: When perpetrators are also victims: latent profiles of traditional and cyberbullying among adolescents who bully in 42 countries
GDC-RR-d1f9996f06.abstract: Background Adolescents who bully others are not a homogeneous group: some confine their behavior to face-to-face settings, whereas others also bully online or are themselves victimized. This study aimed to identify profiles of bullying perpetrators based on their patterns of traditional and cyberbullying perpetration and victimization, and to compare these profiles on individual well-being, health-related risk behaviors, and family, peer, and school characteristics. Methods Data from the 2017/2018 Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study were used. Latent class analysis was used to identify profiles based on indicators of traditional and cyberbullying perpetration and victimization among adolescents who reported bullying others (n = 48,465; 42 countries). Differences between profiles were explored separately for boys and girls using the Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars approach that takes into account classification error. Sensitivity analyses tested the robustness of the solution to alternative specifications of the sample, weighting, measurement, age-group categories, and frequency of bullying. Results Three profiles emerged: a traditional-only profile, a cyber-involved profile characterized by cyberbullying perpetration, and a multiple bully-victim profile of adolescents who both bullied others and were bullied in traditional and cyber contexts. For both genders, the multiple bully-victim profile was the least favorable, with lower levels of perceived health and life satisfaction, increased occurrence of psychosomatic complaints, greater risk behaviors, lower family and peer support, less ease of communication with their mothers, and more negative school experiences. Problematic use of social media increased from the traditional-only to the cyber-involved profile and was greatest in the multiple bully-victim profile. On most other variables, the cyber-involved profile fell between the other two. Sensitivity analyses mostly supported the three-profile solution, although the cyber-involved profile was not recovered using a stricter criterion related to the frequency of bullying behavior. Conclusions The adolescents under study who engage in bullying behaviors do not constitute a homogeneous group; rather they show distinctive involvement patterns. Those who both bully and are bullied across settings fare poorly on several dimensions of their lives and thus interventions and prevention programs should be designed to deal with the different behavioral and psychosocial profiles.

GDC-RR-e923851b08.title: Decoding Digital Risk: Comparing Parent and Teen Reports of Teens' Online Activities.
GDC-RR-e923851b08.authors: Young E, Sharpe JD, Michael S, Welch P, McKinnon II
GDC-RR-e923851b08.abstract: As youth engage with digital media and technologies, parents face evolving challenges in balancing their benefits and risks. Despite recommendations to support parents in promoting teens' healthy digital habits, research suggests that parents' perceptions of teens' online activities often differ from teens' own reports. Using data from 522 parent-teen pairs, this study examined discrepancies in parent versus teen reports of parental digital mediation practices and parental knowledge of teens' online activities. Weighted prevalence estimates and measures of parent-teen discordance were calculated, accounting for the complex survey design. Findings revealed consistent discrepancies, with parents generally overestimating their knowledge of teens' online activities; however, discordance was lowest when parents engaged in digital monitoring strategies. These findings may inform approaches that help parents develop a more accurate understanding of teens' online activities and risk exposure while supporting teens' digital safety and autonomy.

claudeReview.proposedTitle: How much do you really know about what your child does online? A new study suggests less than you think. I include myself.
claudeReview.proposedAngle: I would have told you I had a fair idea what my children do online. A study out this week asked parents and their teenagers the same questions separately and compared the answers, and the parents generally thought they knew more than they did. Stay with the uncomfortable part, which is that it applies to the person writing the post, and be straight about the finding that is awkward for us: the gap was smallest where parents monitored.
claudeReview.oneStory: Researchers compared what parents said about their teenagers' online lives with what the teenagers said themselves, across 522 pairs, and found the parents generally overestimated how much they knew.
claudeReview.oneTension: The gap was smallest in families where parents used digital monitoring. That is awkward for anybody, us included, who says connection matters more than surveillance. And it is still not evidence that monitoring keeps a child safe, because the study measured whether two people gave the same answer, not what happened to the child.
claudeReview.oneBelief: You do not find out what your child does online by assuming you know. You find out by being alongside them, and by asking in a way that makes it easy to tell you. We would rather publish a finding that complicates our own argument than leave it out.
claudeReview.oneTakeaway: Tonight, ask your child one question about what they did online today, and notice whether the answer surprises you.

claims.claim: The study used data from 522 parent and teen pairs.
claims.basis: Stated in the abstract. The abstract also says the estimates were weighted and accounted for a complex survey design, which suggests a survey panel rather than a convenience sample, but it does not name the survey.

claims.claim: Parents generally overestimated their knowledge of their teenagers' online activities.
claims.basis: The abstract's own words: 'consistent discrepancies, with parents generally overestimating their knowledge of teens' online activities'. Verified as what the paper reports. The abstract gives no size for the gap, so it cannot be described as large, small, or any fraction.

claims.claim: The disagreement between parent and teen reports was lowest when parents used digital monitoring strategies.
claims.basis: Stated in the abstract and must be reported, because it is the finding that cuts against our own position. Qualified for three reasons. The abstract does not define 'digital monitoring strategies', so it could mean software, checking a device, or something lighter. The design is a survey at one point in time, so it cannot say monitoring produced the agreement: families who already talk openly may also be the ones who monitor. And agreement between two reports is the outcome, not the child's safety or wellbeing.

claims.claim: Monitoring software keeps teenagers safer online.
claims.basis: The study measured whether parents and teenagers gave matching answers. It did not measure harm, risk exposure outcomes or wellbeing, at least not on the evidence of the abstract.

claims.claim: Parents do not know what their children do online.
claims.basis: Too strong. The finding is that parents on average rate their knowledge higher than their teenagers' answers support. It is a gap, not ignorance, and it is an average across pairs.

claims.claim: The teenager's account is the true one.
claims.basis: The abstract treats the teen report as the reference when it says parents 'overestimate'. A teenager's own report can also be wrong or guarded. The safe wording is that the two accounts differ and the parent's is the more confident one.

claims.claim: This describes UK families.
claims.basis: The abstract does not say where the families live. All five authors are at the Division of Adolescent and School Health at the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the journal is Public Health Reports, so a United States sample is likely, but that is an inference and the full text was not read. Do not describe the sample as American as a fact, and do not carry the finding across to UK families as though it were measured here.

GDC-RR-30c990ff8f.title: Understanding Primary Care Provider Decisions Regarding Referral to Early Intervention for Children with Developmental Delays.
GDC-RR-30c990ff8f.authors: Reinitz MO, Fitzgerald Z, Tangkilisan G, Sanders B, Junqua J, King-Hails L, Solgi M, Zuckerman KE.
GDC-RR-30c990ff8f.abstract:
Objective

While the gap between children identified with developmental conditions and those receiving services has been previously established, less is known regarding the role PCP decision-making plays in service delays.This study aims to explore PCP perspectives on factors influencing their decisions to refer/not refer children with positive developmental screens to Early Intervention (EI) services.

Methods

We conducted qualitative interviews with 15 PCPs from 7 Oregon clinics focusing on general counseling strategies and referral decision making after a positive developmental screen. PCPs were providers who participated in Autism ALERT, a pilot trial of family navigation for children with autism symptoms. Interviews had two parts. Part 1 assessed PCPs' general counseling strategies about Developmental Disabilities (DD) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) screening. Part 2 explored clinical reasoning and management decisions through chart stimulated recall. Each interview was audio recorded and transcribed. Interviews were coded by 2-3 team members using a phenomenological approach to deduce main themes.

Results

Three main interconnected themes and 10 subthemes emerged. Main themes included Screening Tool Results (e.g. severity of results and results reliability), Primary Care Provider's Clinical Judgement (e.g. trust with family and clinical judgement), and Familial Context (e.g. readiness for referral and level of concern). When these three themes were in conflict versus aligned, the decision to refer/not refer was subjected to providers' individual judgement.

Conclusion

Understanding the complexities of EI referral decision making may raise awareness of barriers to referral and improve early referral practices.

GDC-RR-00baf00c43.title: Recent trends of infant motor activity estimation using wearable sensors: A scoping review.
GDC-RR-00baf00c43.authors: DeVito A, Inamdar K, O'Neil ME, Zhu Y, Alam MAU, Koren A.
GDC-RR-00baf00c43.abstract: Wearable sensors may enable objective monitoring of infant motor activity, posture, and movement in laboratory, clinic, and home contexts. However, evidence for the validity, generalizability, and implementation readiness of wearable-derived infant motor measures remains heterogeneous. This scoping review synthesized technical features, validation evidence, and clinical applications of wearable sensors monitoring infant motor activity, posture, or movement during awake periods in the first year of life. PRISMA-ScR guidelines were followed, and the protocol was prospectively registered on Open Science Framework. Searches for peer-reviewed articles on wearable-based monitoring of infant activity published between 2019 and 2024 were identified through searches of PubMed, CINAHL, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library. A total of 41 studies were selected and classified using Keadle's five-phase validation framework, distinguishing technical validation (Phases I-III) from applied implementation (Phase IV). Fifteen studies (36.6%) included typically developing infants, 22 (53.7%) included infants with or at-risk for developmental disabilities, and 4 (9.8%) were unspecified. Fifteen studies (36.6%) focused on technical validation; 26 (63.4%) implemented sensors in applied contexts. Triaxial accelerometers (n = 15) and IMUs (n = 24) were most common, with sampling frequencies from 1-150 Hz. Posture classification accuracy was 95.8%-98.2% in studies directly comparing posture and movement, whereas fine-grained movement classification was near 81%-84%. Reference-standard correspondence was generally strong for accumulated posture duration (r = 0.80-0.99) but more variable for movement and clinical measures (r = 0.61-0.98). Application studies quantified physical activity, movement coordination and complexity, and intervention responsiveness, with over half collecting home-based data. Wearable sensors have evolved from proof-of-concept systems to family-centered digital health tools supporting developmental monitoring and physical activity promotion. When paired with caregiver feedback and infant-centered design, these technologies may support families, complement clinic-based assessment, and extend developmental support access. Future research should prioritize standardized reporting, affordability, and open-source analytic pipelines to advance equitable implementation.

GDC-RR-ce0516cd06.title: THE IMPACT OF GLOBAL YOUTH MOVEMENTS ON INDIAN YOUTH (2020–OCTOBER 2026) A Sociological Study of Political Consciousness, Digital Activism and Social Change
GDC-RR-ce0516cd06.abstract: A new wave of youth movements has emerged globally in the third decade of the twenty-first century. Between 2020 and October 2026, young people in various countries staged large-scale protests against corruption, unemployment, inflation, weaknesses in education systems, the crisis of political representation, social inequality, human-rights violations and restrictions on freedom of expression. A distinctive feature of these movements has been the important role played not only by traditional organisations but also by social media, digital networks, online campaigns and decentralised leadership. Youth activism in Myanmar, Thailand, the United States, Nigeria, Sri Lanka, Iran, Bangladesh, Kenya, Indonesia, Nepal, Serbia, Morocco, Madagascar, the Philippines and European countries such as France, Italy and Spain has influenced political and social debates. By October 2026, the movements emerging in Europe had foregrounded the quality of education, the housing crisis, the rising cost of living, employment insecurity and the condition of public services. This research article presents a sociological study of the possible effects of global youth movements on Indian youth by analysing their nature, causes, forms and consequences. It uses the theories of relative deprivation, resource mobilisation and new social movements, along with the concept of the network society. The study concludes that global youth movements can encourage political awareness, sensitivity towards civil rights, digital participation and aspirations for social change among young people. However, the success of a movement is not confined to protests; it also requires democratic institutions, policy reforms and sustained social participation

GDC-RR-bafc7bb71a.title: National support for a healthy checkout policy: a randomised message-framing experiment.
GDC-RR-bafc7bb71a.authors: Gil AM, Reimold AE, Lemmon B, Wolf EC, Dorfman L, Brown SD, Au LE, Falbe J.
GDC-RR-bafc7bb71a.abstract:
Objective

Healthy checkout policies set nutritional standards for store checkouts and have been implemented in three US jurisdictions. We compared four message frames, each describing a different rationale for the policy, on adults' support for a healthy checkout policy.

Design

Participants were randomised to one of four message frames: (1) expanding healthy choices; (2) reducing parental stress by removing unhealthy items from child eye level; (3) improving community and child health; or (4) addressing predatory marketing. We used Poisson regression with robust standard errors to examine policy support by message frame and explore variation in support by socio-demographic characteristics.

Setting

Online randomised experiment.

Participants

A convenience sample of US adults (analytic N 3978) recruited online via quota-matching to approximate national socio-demographic characteristics.

Results

Overall, most participants (65 %) supported a healthy checkout policy. Support was moderately higher (68 %) when the policy was framed as reducing parental stress than addressing predatory marketing (64 %) or expanding healthy choices (61 %; all p < 0·05). Policy support was also higher when framed as improving community and child health (67 %) than expanding healthy choices (61 %; p < 0·01). In adjusted models, overall policy support was higher among adults with Hispanic ethnicity (68 %); incomes >$35 000 (range 66-70 %); a prediabetes or type 2 diabetes diagnosis (67 %); at least some college education (67 %) and residence in the Northeast US (70 %; all p < 0·05).

Conclusions

Support for a healthy checkout policy was high, especially when framed around benefits to child health. Adults with certain socio-demographic and clinical characteristics may especially support healthy checkout policies.

GDC-RR-e0121857da.title: Religious Communities and Social Media in North Macedonia: Between Digital Presence and Online Engagement
GDC-RR-e0121857da.authors: Aleksandar Grizhev, Ivan Blazhevski, Ruzica Cacanoska
GDC-RR-e0121857da.abstract: Religious communities increasingly operate within digital environments where institutional communication, religious practice, and audience interaction intersect. Yet, establishing a presence on social media does not necessarily translate into meaningful engagement or dialogue. This study examines how the principal religious communities in North Macedonia use social media platforms and how their institutional communication practices are reflected in the digital public sphere. Drawing on an exploratory qualitative content analysis conducted between January and June 2025, this research examines institutional and institutionally associated Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube accounts of the principal religious communities in the country while considering selected smaller communities where relevant. The analysis focuses on platform presence, posting practices, types of content, language use, multimedia formats, institutional organization, and patterns of interaction with followers. The findings reveal substantial differences in the visibility, intensity, and sophistication of digital communication across religious communities. However, despite greater use of multimedia, multilingual communication, and more frequent posting among some actors, communication remains predominantly oriented toward dissemination rather than sustained dialogue. More interactive practices are observed mainly in youth-oriented and community-focused accounts. This study argues that digital presence, dissemination, engagement, and dialogue should be understood as distinct but overlapping dimensions of institutional religious communication. It also contributes to the study of digital religion by examining these dynamics in a religiously plural Southeast European context.

claudeReview.proposedTitle: The government asked its own scientists whether social media harms children. Their answer was that nobody has run the experiment.
claudeReview.proposedAngle: I do not know whether social media is damaging children's mental health at the scale people say. What I did not expect was that the scientists the government commissioned would say much the same thing, in a report it published this January. Walk a parent or a head through what the report found, what it could not find, and what it asked for, without turning it into ammunition for either side.
claudeReview.oneStory: A consortium of UK academics commissioned by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology reviewed the evidence on time spent on social media and adolescent mental health, and found a small, consistent link, low certainty that it is causal, and no experiment in healthy adolescents that tests it.
claudeReview.oneTension: There is a link, and it shows up again and again. And the people best placed to judge it say they still cannot tell whether social media is the cause, because the studies that would settle it have not been done.
claudeReview.oneBelief: The response should be in proportion to the evidence, and that cuts both ways. Low certainty is not proof of harm and it is not proof of safety. It is a reason to act on what a family can see in front of them rather than wait for a verdict.
claudeReview.oneTakeaway: When somebody tells you the science is settled in either direction, ask them which experiment settled it. In January the government's own report said there was not one.

claims.claim: The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology commissioned the report to explore how research on the causal relationship between digital technology use and population level outcomes for children and adolescents can be improved.
claims.basis: Stated in the executive summary. The funder statement adds that the policy team set the scope and gave feedback on a draft, and did not inform the results or conclusions.

claims.claim: The report is the work of a scientific consortium of 14 UK academics across 10 universities.
claims.basis: The methodology section says 'a Scientific Consortium across 10 universities and 14 leading academics in the UK'. The recommended citation lists 18 authors, because it includes the research staff. So write 14 academics in the consortium, never 14 authors and never 18 scientists.

claims.claim: Seven systematic reviews examined time spent on social media and adolescent mental health. One was rated high quality and six were rated critically low.
claims.basis: Key finding 1 of the evidence review: 'The methodological quality ranged from critically low (n = 6) to high (n = 1)', assessed with an adapted AMSTAR 2 tool. The executive summary says the same in words: 'Only one review, out of seven, was found to be of high quality.'

claims.claim: Across those reviews there was consistent evidence of a small association between more time on social media and poorer adolescent mental health, and the association also appeared in longitudinal data.
claims.basis: Key finding 1 and the executive summary. This claim has to appear in any copy that uses the report. Leaving it out would turn 'low certainty about cause' into 'no evidence of a link', which the report does not say.

claims.claim: The certainty that the association is causal is low.
claims.basis: Key finding 2 is headed 'Low certainty of causality' and gives the reasons: most primary studies were cross sectional, relied on self report and lacked diverse samples, confounding may explain the association, and reverse causality cannot be ruled out. The executive summary says the ability to determine a causal impact at population level 'remains poor'.

claims.claim: No experimental study has tested whether reducing time on social media improves mental health or wellbeing in healthy adolescents.
claims.basis: True of what the consortium found: 'we found no experimental studies on healthy adolescents that sought to reduce time spent on social media'. Two qualifications, both required. First, the same paragraph of key finding 2 says experiments on social media and screen time reduction 'show some benefits to mental health and wellbeing', but none of them was in healthy adolescents. Second, the work was produced between December 2024 and March 2025, so trials may have started or reported since. Write it with the date and in the past tense.

claims.claim: The evidence synthesis found no reviews on the effect of time spent on smartphones, or on AI chat applications, on adolescent mental health and wellbeing.
claims.basis: Stated twice in the executive summary. Same date qualification as above.

claims.claim: For school phone restrictions, the evidence was more consistent for behaviour in school than for mental health and wellbeing.
claims.basis: Executive summary: more consistent for in school behaviours such as screen time in school, bullying and physical activity, 'less robust and more context-dependent' for mental health and wellbeing.

claims.claim: The report shows that social media does not harm children.
claims.basis: The report says the opposite of this in its second paragraph of substance: harms to individual children are documented and 'require urgent attention'. Its subject is a different question, the average effect across the whole population, and on that its finding is low certainty, not absence of harm.

claims.claim: The report recommends that developing and testing interventions that help individuals, families, schools and communities navigate the digital environment should also be seen as a priority.
claims.basis: The wording is in recommendation 4 and is quoted accurately. It is qualified because it is the one line in the report that flatters what we sell, so it gets more scrutiny, not less. It is a recommendation about what research should be funded, it says 'developing and testing', and nothing we have built has been tested in that sense. It is not an endorsement of any product and must never be written as one.

claims.basis: The report takes no position on an age restriction and does not advise for or against one. Its closing line asks for evidence 'to drive, not delay' effective responses. What ministers read, and when, is not something this document can tell us.

It is dated. The work was done between December 2024 and March 2025, the cover says May 2025, and it reached GOV.UK on 20 January 2026. Anything published since is outside it.
Only seven reviews met its criteria, and it judged six of them critically low quality, so its own conclusions rest on thin ground and it says so.
Its focus is 'time spent', which the report itself calls an overly simple measure. Content, timing and what the time displaces may matter more.
Its question is the average effect across a population. It says in terms that this is distinct from harm to an individual child, which it treats as documented and urgent.
The 'healthy adolescents' restriction is the consortium's own pre set focus. Experiments in other groups exist and showed some benefit.
Appendices 2 to 8 were searched, not read line by line, in this review.
contradictoryEvidence: The report's own key finding 1 is the strongest thing against a 'nothing to see' reading: a small, consistent association, present in longitudinal data too, with increased use appearing to come before declines in mental health in some studies.

The report cites the argument that the rise in symptoms of poor mental health coincides in time with the arrival of smartphones and social media in the early 2010s. It does not dismiss that argument. It says the parallel fuelled the debate and that the causal question is hard to assess.

whatThisDoesNotProve: That social media is harmless, for children in general or for any one child.
That social media causes mental health problems. The report says the certainty of that is low.
That an age restriction will or will not work. The report does not test one.
That anything we build helps. The report asks for interventions of this kind to be developed and tested. Ours has not been tested.
Anything about what has been learned since early 2025.

Any copy we produce has to hold both halves: a small consistent link, and low certainty about cause.
gdcBeliefs: The Wrong Villain: the response should be in proportion to the evidence, and that cuts both ways.
A deadline is not a plan. Whatever the law does, a family still needs something to do on a Tuesday night, and that does not wait for a trial to report.
'Screen time' is not one exposure. The report says the same about 'time spent'.
Evidence or silence: we say plainly that we hold no outcome evidence for our own product.

productImplications.schoolLesson: The school phone finding, better evidence for behaviour in school than for wellbeing, is worth knowing before any school pitch that leans on wellbeing. Do not promise wellbeing gains from a phone policy or from our lessons.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) is the UK’s independent regulator for information rights
legislation. This includes the Data Protection Act 2018 and the UK General Data Protection Regulation
(UKGDPR). In September 2021, the ICO’s Age Appropriate Design Code (AADC or Children’s code), a
statutory code, came into force. This requires organisations which are offering online services likely to be
accessed by children to conform to 15 standards. Standard three of the code sets an expectation that online
platforms either establish the age of their users with an appropriate degree of certainty, or apply the standards
in the code to all users.
Ofcom has a statutory duty to promote and research media literacy, including in respect of material available on
the internet. A key way it seeks to fulfil this duty is through its Making Sense of Media programme, which aims
to help improve the online skills, knowledge and understanding of children and adults in the UK. Ofcom was
also given powers in autumn 2020 to regulate UK-established video-sharing platforms (VSPs). And in December
2020, the Government confirmed its intention to nominate Ofcom as the regulator for online safety in the UK,
under the Online Safety Bill.
The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) brings together four UK regulators tasked with regulating
digital services to collectively drive greater regulatory co-operation and deliver coherent approaches to digital
regulation. Through the DRCF workplan for 2022-23, the ICO and Ofcom committed to working together on
protecting children online and synchronising their efforts – with a particular focus on improving outcomes for
children and parents – by ensuring privacy and online safety protections work in unison. This includes joint
research on age assurance, as well as a joint working framework to support the oversight of Ofcom’s Video
Sharing Platform (VSP) regulatory framework and the ICO’s Children’s code.
This research will also inform Ofcom’s preparations for implementing the new online safety laws, as referenced
in Ofcom’s Roadmap to Online Safety Regulation. As part of these preparations, Ofcom is building a robust
evidence base, bringing together internal and external data, collected using different methods, from a variety of
different sources. This programme of research will further develop Ofcom’s understanding of online harms and
how it can help to promote a safer user experience.
Age Assurance Research
Age assurance refers to a number of measures which would allow organisations to prevent children from
accessing services which are inappropriate for their age, and also to tailor services to suit their developmental
needs 1.

Ofcom as age assurance products that comply with data protection legislation and meet further online safety

This research provides an understanding of the attitudes parents and children have about age assurance. The
research shows there is parental and child support for the principle of age assurance, but also recognises some

claudeReview.reviewBasis: The full text, held in the register cache (digest cdf32d71 checked against the register before reading). Read in full: the preface, the executive summary, the background and methodology, the passages in sections 1 and 3 on circumvention and on how parents oversee use, the conclusions, and the start of the methodology annex. The GOV.UK publication page was resolved through the content API, which gives the published date as 11 October 2022.
claudeReview.proposedTitle: The regulators asked families about age checks. They found that parents were often the ones helping children past them.
claudeReview.proposedAngle: I do not know whether the new age checks will hold. What I do know is what the regulators found the last time they sat in families' homes and asked: most of the children had got past the age check or knew someone who had, the parents often knew, and some had helped. Do not write this as a telling off. Write it as a parent who recognises the reasoning, because the report explains why parents did it, and the reason is the story.
claudeReview.oneStory: In 2022 the ICO and Ofcom commissioned researchers to spend time with families and ask about age checks. The researchers found most children had got round them or knew someone who had, that parents were often aware, and that some parents had helped, for example by telling a child to enter a different date of birth.
claudeReview.oneTension: Parents told the researchers they wanted age checks to exist. The same parents were not enforcing the ones that did exist, because an age limit that takes no account of their own child felt arbitrary and saying no meant their child being the one left out.
claudeReview.oneBelief: A rule that a family does not believe in does not get kept at home, whatever the law says. A deadline is not a plan. What changes behaviour is a parent who has decided, with their child, what this child is ready for and why.
claudeReview.oneTakeaway: Before the next age limit arrives, decide what you actually think your child is ready for and say it to them in your own words. A rule you can explain is one you will keep.

claims.claim: The research was qualitative: in depth interviews with 18 families in their homes, and 8 focus groups, 4 with parents and 4 with children aged 13 to 17, carried out from May to August 2022.
claims.basis: Executive summary and methodology. The home visits lasted about four hours each and were preceded by a three day media diary. The research was carried out by an independent agency, Revealing Reality.

claims.claim: Most children in the study had got round age assurance themselves, typically by entering a false age, or knew someone who had.
claims.basis: The report's own words: 'Most children had circumvented current age assurance methods themselves (typically self-declaration on social media platforms) or knew someone who had.' Qualified because 'most' here means most of a small, deliberately varied qualitative sample. It is not a national rate and must never be given a percentage.

claims.claim: Parents were often aware of this, and some had helped.
claims.basis: Executive summary: 'parents were often aware of this, and sometimes facilitated it'. Section 1 gives the example of telling a child to use an incorrect date of birth, and section 3 says some parents 'were happy to set up children's accounts using their own information, including their age'. The section heading in the conclusions reads 'many parents were allowing, and even facilitating, their children to circumvent current age assurance measures'.

claims.claim: Many parents saw the minimum ages on social media and games as arbitrary, and wanted stronger checks for gambling, pornography and buying alcohol than for social media.
claims.basis: Executive summary and conclusions. Parents weighed their own child's maturity and their own sense of the risk, not only the child's age.

claims.claim: Parents often put good communication with their child ahead of other ways of overseeing what they did online.
claims.basis: Executive summary: 'parents often felt that maintaining good communication with their child about their online behaviours was a high priority over other methods'. This is the line that meets our own position, so it is quoted exactly and not stretched: it reports what parents said they valued, not what works.

claims.claim: As children get older, parents become less motivated and less able to monitor or restrict, and children become more motivated and more able to get round controls.
claims.basis: Executive summary, section 3. The ways children got round controls included reaching parents' settings, opening new accounts when a parent followed the first, and using a VPN.

claims.claim: Parents and children saw a passport or driving licence as the most effective way to check age.
claims.basis: Executive summary. It matters because it cuts against a lazy reading: these families did not think age checks were pointless, they thought self declaration was.

claims.claim: A given percentage of UK parents help their children lie about their age.
claims.basis: This study cannot give a percentage. It is 18 families and 8 groups. Any national figure would have to come from separate survey research, which was not read in this run.

claims.claim: Age checks do not work, so the under 16 restriction will fail.
claims.basis: The fieldwork was in 2022, when the usual check was typing in a date of birth. The law and the methods have both changed since. The study describes how families behaved towards weak checks they did not believe in. It says nothing about how they will behave towards stronger ones.

claims.claim: Ofcom and the ICO say parents help children get round age checks.
claims.basis: The report states that it 'represents the views of research participants obtained through the commissioned research, and not those of the ICO or Ofcom'. The correct attribution is research commissioned by the ICO and Ofcom and carried out by Revealing Reality. Never 'Ofcom says' or 'the ICO found'. GOV.UK lists the page under the Competition and Markets Authority because of the regulators' joint forum. Do not attribute it to that body either.

From the same report: most parents felt services should have age assurance measures. The finding is a tension, not a rejection.

The context has changed since the fieldwork. Services are now under legal duties to use stronger age assurance, so behaviour found in 2022 may not carry over. This is context, not a study, and no claim about how well the new checks work is cleared.

That age checks cannot work, or that the under 16 restriction will fail.
That parents who helped were wrong to. The report does not judge them and neither do we.
That talking to your child works better than controls. Parents said they valued it more. The study did not measure outcomes.
Anything about how families behave under the rules in force today.

productImplications.parentTool: The stage check is the proof path: three questions about one child that give a parent a view of their own on what the child is ready for, which is exactly what the parents in this research were weighing when they called age limits arbitrary. No outcome is claimed.
productImplications.digi: When a parent asks whether to let a child sign up under age, DiGi must not allow or deny. This report supports the calibrated answer: what is your child ready for, what would you want in place, and what will you say to them.

GDC-RR-e1a6cd5229.title: Changes in family structure and children's screen time: a longitudinal study of Australian children.
GDC-RR-e1a6cd5229.authors: Shifera N, Pagano R, Sanders T.
GDC-RR-e1a6cd5229.abstract:
Children's screen time varies by family structure, but evidence remains cross-sectional, making it difficult to determine whether differences reflect family structure or pre-existing sociodemographic inequalities. To our knowledge, no study has used matched comparison groups to test whether screen time changes following family transitions (two-parent to single-parent and vice versa). Using data from the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children, a nationally representative study drawing on the Baby and Kindergarten cohorts to follow children aged 6 to 13 (N = 8706 at baseline; mean age, 6.86 years; 51% male; 85% in two-parent households), we used pre-registered multilevel mixed-effects models to examine associations between family structure, sibling number, and screen time, and propensity score-matched piecewise regression to test changes in screen time following family transitions. After full adjustment, living in a single-parent household was not significantly associated with screen time (B = 11.98 min/week; 95% CI, - 7.41 to 31.37). Transitions from two-parent to single-parent (B = 18.45 min/week; 95% CI, - 94.48 to 131.39) or from single-parent to two-parent (B = - 49.47 min/week; 95% CI, - 247.58 to 148.64) were not associated with changes in screen time. In contrast, each additional sibling was associated with lower screen time (B = - 22.71 min/week; 95% CI, - 30.18 to - 15.25).

Conclusion

The association between family structure and screen time is largely explained by sociodemographic factors, and family transitions do not produce significant changes in screen time. Interventions to reduce screen time may be better directed at sociodemographic inequalities rather than at family structure or transitions, while considering siblings.

What is known

• Most evidence on family structure and children's screen time is cross-sectional, leaving unclear whether family structure or pre-existing family differences explain observed patterns. • No study has used matched comparison groups to examine whether children's screen time trajectories shift following a family structure transition.

What is new

• Screen time levels and trajectories were compared before and after transitions in both directions, between children who transitioned and matched children in stable households. • After adjustment, family structure was not associated with screen time, and transitions were not associated with changes in screen time; having more siblings was consistently associated with lower screen time.

GDC-RR-477a38762a.title: English immersive game participation and attention, emotional health, and cognitive function in children: a cross-sectional study
GDC-RR-477a38762a.abstract: Background Screen exposure is an important issue for children’s health. The existing research pays more attention to the duration of use, but not to the content type and immersion experience. English immersion game integrates language learning and game mechanism, which belongs to educational digital behavior. This study analyzes the daily English game duration, immersion and English integration of children aged 6–14, and their relationships with attention, working memory, executive function and emotional behavior. Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included 215 children. Based on the parents’ questionnaire, the data of English game participation were obtained: daily duration, 1–5 immersion self-evaluation, and English integration. The outcome includes all kinds of attention, working memory, executive function, emotion and ADHD symptoms. Multivariate linear regression controls total screen time, sleep, physical activity, age, gender and family SES. CPT, Flanker and Corsi were the main outcomes, and after Bonferroni correction, the four executive function and behavior indicators were set as exploratory outcomes, which were not corrected. Results English game time is positively correlated with selective attention ( β = 0.218, p = 0.001). It is significantly different from the primary analysis of working memory, and its effect size fell below the minimum-detectable-effect threshold following Bonferroni correction. Immersion self-rating is positively correlated with multiple attention and working memory, and negatively correlated with emotional symptoms. The degree of English integration is positively correlated with cognitive indicators and negatively correlated with emotional symptoms; After excluding the pure-English-immersion subgroup, the association with selective attention and inhibition control is no longer significant, and it is regarded as descriptive association. Daily screen time was negatively correlated with cognitive ability, and positively correlated with mood and ADHD symptoms (all p &lt; 0.001). Conclusion Different dimensions of English immersion games are related to children’s cognitive and emotional outcomes. In addition to the duration of use, the integration of game English is as important as the immersion experience. The results can provide reference for family digital activity selection, children’s screen behavior norms and campus digital education intervention, which still needs to be verified by longitudinal research.

GDC-RR-145e62ea60.title: Atomoxetine-associated Raynaud’s phenomenon in children: an under-recognized risk of non-stimulant ADHD therapy
GDC-RR-145e62ea60.authors: Wenxiu Mo, Lin Liu, Zheyu Cui, Yan Li, Huawei Mao
GDC-RR-145e62ea60.abstract: Raynaud’s phenomenon (RP) is an increasingly recognized yet still underreported adverse effect of ADHD pharmacotherapy. Whereas stimulant-associated RP is well documented, atomoxetine-related RP has surfaced only in isolated pediatric cases, leaving a gap in our understanding of non-stimulant toxicity. This narrative review reports the first Asian pediatric case identified in English- and regional-language literature and synthesizes the global evidence base, integrating five pediatric cases, targeted literature retrieval, and disproportionality analyses of FAERS and WHO VigiBase. Atomoxetine carries a consistent pharmacovigilance signal for RP. Beyond the elevation of synaptic cleft norepinephrine, the five cases point to suspected contributors: plasma drug concentration, CYP2D6-mediated metabolic variability—particularly relevant in East Asian populations—and individual susceptibility with superimposed triggers. Onset latency is highly variable (hours to years), and the course in reported cases is milder and fully reversible, without digital ulceration, features consistent with, though not determined by, the sustained, gradual peripheral noradrenergic elevation produced by selective norepinephrine transporter inhibition, in contrast to the rapid catecholamine surges typical of stimulants. These findings call for longitudinal vigilance beyond the titration phase, prompt exclusion of secondary causes, and systematic pharmacovigilance reporting.

GDC-RR-6ea01c5e1a.abstract: Introduction Despite expanding artificial intelligence (AI) research, evidence remains fragmented on how AI capacity, Human-Capital Transformation, institutions, and labor-market structure jointly relate to unequal development. Methods Using 229 country-year observations from 50 purposively selected economies over 2020–2024, this study integrates conceptual development, composite measurement, panel estimation, country configurations, and conditional projections for 2026–2027. Moving beyond traditional productivist paradigms, this study conceptualizes adaptive human capital (AHC) as the dynamic capacity to preserve, renew, recombine, and redeploy human capabilities under technological change, with health sustaining adaptability, lifelong learning enabling renewal, and skills recalibration supporting resilience. This model distinguishes adaptive capacity from its observable educational and digital foundations. Five author-constructed indices capture AI Diffusion Capacity (AIDC), Human-Capital Transformation (HCT), Enabling Conditions, AI-Related Labor-Market Pressure, and multidimensional Development Outcomes. Two-way fixed-effects models use country-clustered standard errors, restricted wild-cluster-bootstrap inference, and false-discovery-rate correction. Sensitivity checks examine alternative weights, component exclusion, and 1,000 positive random-weight draws. Results AIDC coefficients are positive for HCT (β = 0.220, p = 0.0063) and Development Outcomes (β = 0.160, p = 0.027), although the latter attenuates after income adjustment. The strongest results concern labor absorption: negative AIDC coefficients for total unemployment (β = −0.359) and youth unemployment (β = −0.319) and a positive coefficient for the employment-to-population ratio (β = 0.258) remain significant after income adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. Comparisons among similar AIDC countries identify configuration-level heterogeneity without a consistently dominant human-capital, institutional, or labor-market correlate. Complementary AIDC–HCT and AIDC–unemployment maps distinguish aligned and asymmetric country configurations; the latter classifies 14, 12, 11, and 13 economies into four labor-market groups. Conditional joint AIDC–HCT paths imply declining Development Outcomes under the lower scenario and improving outcomes under the central and upper scenarios; separate AIDC paths map labor-configuration transitions. Discussion Unequal development is reflected in asymmetric technological and labor-market configurations: 12 countries combine above-average AIDC with above-median unemployment, whereas 11 combine below-average AIDC with unemployment at or below the sample median of 4.545%. The study connects an adaptive human-capital framework with differentiated empirical evidence on technological capacity, human capabilities, and labor absorption, informing country-specific priorities for technological scaling, capability renewal, and support during labor-market transitions.

GDC-RR-063230519e.title: Scaffolding young children’s AI use: opening pedagogical black boxes in early childhood classrooms
GDC-RR-063230519e.authors: Xinyun Hu, Boris Wai Yan Choy
GDC-RR-063230519e.abstract: Abstract Given their real-time responsive capabilities, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have been positioned as cognitive partners for young children. However, research and policy directives have tended toward technological determinism, which black-boxes how these technologies function in early childhood education (ECE). Applying Actor-Network Theory (ANT), this qualitative case study deconstructs pedagogical black boxes during a plant inquiry unit involving a teacher, four children (aged 5–6), and AI-integrated devices. The findings provide a typology of three pedagogical black boxes: operational (obscuring technical constraints), epistemic (obscuring knowledge construction), and relational (obscuring negotiations of agency and classroom authority). Analysis of the case illustrated how these black boxes opened through distance (children’s communication gaps), breakdown (AI errors), and innovation (negotiation over AI use), revealing hidden dynamics in AI integration, such as uncertainty, people at work, decisions, competition, and controversies. Teacher scaffolding emerged as a key mediator of child-AI interactions, translating children’s open-ended inquiries into AI-legible inputs, transforming AI errors into opportunities for evaluative judgement, and recalibrating children’s AI interactions into child-led scientific inquiry. Ultimately, the paper shows that the seamless integration of AI is neither realistic nor pedagogically effective, and exemplifies how emergent frictions can foster young learners’ AI literacy, evaluative judgement, and relational agency.

GDC-RR-3525014c5a.title: Community-based Screening for Autism Spectrum Disorder Among Children in Pondicherry: A Cross-sectional Study
GDC-RR-3525014c5a.journal: Journal of Indian Association for Child and Adolescent Mental Health
GDC-RR-3525014c5a.authors: Bhavani S, Sarah Catherine S, Nishanth Rajan, Priya Jose, Peter Prasanth Kumar K, Shanthi Kannan
GDC-RR-3525014c5a.abstract: Background: Most Indian studies on Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) are hospital-based, and community-level data using standardized screening tools remain limited. Community screening can help identify children at risk and generate hypotheses regarding associated factors. The main objective of the study was to screen for ASD among children in Pondicherry and to identify associated factors. Methods: A community-based cross-sectional screening study was conducted in rural and urban areas of Pondicherry between September 2023 and February 2024. Children aged 18 months to 14 years ( n = 272) were screened using the AIIMS-modified INCLEN diagnostic tool for ASD. Participants were recruited using convenience sampling. Socio-demographic details and information on perinatal, familial, environmental, and behavioral factors were collected through parental interviews. Environmental variables such as ventilation and overcrowding were self-reported. The proportion of screen-positive ASD was calculated. Associations between screen-positive ASD and various factors were explored using Fisher’s exact test and Mann–Whitney U test. Results: Seven children were found to be screen-positive for ASD, yielding a proportion of 2.57% (95% CI: 1.03%-5.26%) in this screened sample. Screen-positive ASD showed significant associations with male gender ( P = .006), age group 5–10 years ( P = .04), late preterm birth ( P = .013), respiratory distress at birth ( P = .015), and reduced time spent in outdoor play ( P = .033). Other socio-demographic, familial, and environmental variables did not show significant associations. These findings represent unadjusted exploratory associations. Conclusion: This community-based screening study identified a small proportion of children who screened positive for ASD and highlighted several factors that showed exploratory associations. The findings underscore the importance of community screening and the need for larger, methodologically robust studies to estimate the proportion and evaluate risk factors for ASD in the Indian context.

GDC-RR-6079ade78d.title: Multiscale Evaluation of Quercetin Against Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Vibrio vulnificus in Seafood and Food-Contact Surfaces
GDC-RR-6079ade78d.authors: Nigar Sultana Meghla, Md Furkanur Rahaman Mizan, Syeda Roufun Nesa, Sangha Han, Iksoon Kang, Sang-Do Ha
GDC-RR-6079ade78d.abstract: Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Vibrio vulnificus biofilms pose a major challenge to seafood safety owing to their persistence on food-contact surfaces and increased tolerance to antimicrobial interventions. This study investigated the antibiofilm efficacy and mechanisms of quercetin using integrated structural, physiological, and molecular approaches. Quercetin exhibited concentration-dependent biofilm inhibition and reduced mature biofilms on abiotic surfaces, while its efficacy in inhibiting biofilm formation was evaluated on seafood. Quercetin suppressed early biofilm establishment by reducing cell surface hydrophobicity, bacterial adhesion, autoaggregation, motility, cellular respiration, and ATP production, thereby limiting bacterial attachment and microcolony formation. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy revealed changes in the EPS-associated spectral profiles of both species, indicating alterations in the biochemical composition of the biofilm matrix. These spectral changes varied between V. vulnificus and V. parahaemolyticus. Gene expression analysis demonstrated coordinated downregulation of quorum sensing (QS), adhesion, and EPS biosynthesis genes, accompanied by increased membrane permeability, intracellular protein leakage, and metabolic dysfunction. In a 6 h screen, 1/2 MIC caused only minor changes in the color and texture of shrimp and oyster, whereas MIC caused larger changes; no cytotoxicity was detected under the tested conditions. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that quercetin disrupts Vibrio biofilms through coordinated mechanisms with limited short-term effects on seafood color and texture at 1/2 MIC, supporting further evaluation as a natural, industry-relevant strategy for controlling seafood-associated Vibrio biofilms and improving seafood safety.

GDC-RR-7e9b72deec.title: A blended digital parenting intervention for the prevention of sexual violence, exploitative sex, and maltreatment of children at scale in Tanzania: a cluster-randomised, controlled trial.
GDC-RR-7e9b72deec.authors: Cluver LD, Ornellas A, Klapwijk JM, Nyalali K, Chetty AN, Mgunga S, Melendez-Torres GJ, Kahwa J, Awah I, Baerecke L, Booij A, Christine L, de Graaf K, Lachman JM, Markle L, Mjwara SN, Stern D, Te Winkel E, Tsoanyane S, Sherr L, Wambura M, Green O, Ngcobo L, Mwakakeke S, Desmond C, Clements L, Kijoti E, Manjengenja N, Wamoyi J.
GDC-RR-7e9b72deec.abstract: Childhood sexual, physical, and verbal violence are global public health priorities, affecting 1 billion children each year. ParentApp integrates sexual violence prevention into WHO-UNICEF's open-access Parenting for Lifelong Health programme, using innovative blended digital delivery. We aimed to test the efficacy of ParentApp in preventing sexual violence and maltreatment against adolescent-aged children and improving preventive mechanisms such as family mental health and adolescent-caregiver relationships. This cluster-randomised, controlled trial was conducted in 80 Tanzanian sub-wards. Participants were primary caregivers aged 18 years and older and their adolescents (aged 10-17 years). Sub-wards were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either ParentApp (intervention group) or a control WASHApp programme. Clusters were randomly assigned in blocks of six, stratified by urban versus rural location. Statisticians carrying out randomisation and data analysts were masked; it was not possible to mask participants or researchers. Intervention groups received a low-cost Android phone installed with ParentApp, a 12-module offline-first app, with one in-person orientation session and remote support via WhatsApp group chats, at a delivery cost of US$6 per family at scale, or $10 with 20% smartphone provision. Control groups received a low-cost Android phone installed with WASHApp, a 12-module offline-first app for water, sanitation, and hygiene, with one in-person orientation session. The primary outcomes were adolescent sexual violence victimisation and maltreatment and high-risk situations for sexual violence, assessed in all participants irrespective of uptake and engagement at 5 months and 18 months post-baseline. The trial was registered on March 14, 2023, with OSF (https://osf.io/t9fxz) and is completed. Between May 11 and Oct 9, 2023, 2692 caregiver-adolescent dyads were screened for study eligibility; 2396 adolescents (1217 [50·8%] female and 1179 [49·2%] male) and 2396 caregivers (1795 [74·9%] female and 601 [25·1%] male) were recruited. 2145 (89·5%) adolescents and 2252 (94·0%) caregivers were retained in the study and included in analyses at 18 months. Adolescent girls in ParentApp clusters had a substantial reduction in past-month sexual violence victimisation compared with those in control clusters (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0·43 [95% CI 0·21-0·86]; p=0·018), with no effect for boys (1·21 [0·59-2·43]; p=0·60). Past-month maltreatment (physical abuse, verbal abuse, and neglect) was lower in ParentApp clusters than in control clusters (adolescent report IRR 0·92 [0·88-0·96]; p<0·0001, caregiver report 0·87 [0·82-0·92]; p<0·0001). Past-month exposure to high-risk situations for sexual violence was lower in ParentApp clusters than in control clusters (adolescent girls IRR 0·87 [0·77-0·97]; p=0·012, adolescent boys 0·85 [0·79-0·91]; p<0·0001, caregiver report 0·81 [0·75-0·88]; p<0·0001). There were no reported adverse events. A low-cost blended digital parenting programme in countries such as Tanzania could simultaneously reduce childhood sexual violence (for girls) and maltreatment and sexual violence risk situations (for girls and boys). GDC-RR-bfd4ff8bf4.title: Scaling guided play through educational media: bridging theory and practice across diverse global contexts
GDC-RR-bfd4ff8bf4.authors: Kim Foulds, Jennifer M. Zosh, Rosemarie Truglio, Jessica DiSalvo, Shanna Kohn, Autumn Zitani
GDC-RR-bfd4ff8bf4.abstract: This paper explores the intersection of theory and industry practice, examining how educational media leverages playful learning to facilitate transfer of learning in children living in diverse global contexts. Central to this discussion is the evolution of Sesame Street , highlighting its strategic shift toward utilizing guided play models. We ground this discussion in Esme &amp; Roy , an animated series that established Sesame Workshop's approach to modeling guided play on screen and show how that approach shaped two future productions: the playful “approaches to learning” curriculum of Sesame Street Seasons 51–52, and Watch, Play, Learn , a suite of early learning videos designed to support children affected by crisis and conflict. Together, these examples demonstrate how intentional media design can support transfer of learning across varied geographic contexts and how theory informs practice, which then further refines theory. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these advancements for the future of educational media and playful learning.
